extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and scientometricians interested in open peer review and open science policy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and characterizing implementations of open peer review (OPR) in scholarly journals, including which OPR elements are present, how they are implemented, and metrics for adoption and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Open identities may include reviewer names and affiliation as well as credentials; open identities may be mandated, optional (decided by the reviewer), or anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open identities are one of the two core elements defining OPR transparency. Requiring reviewer identification may encourage accountability but could blunt criticisms; allowing choice may increase reviewer willingness. When assessing OPR, record whether identities are required, optional, or anonymous and whether names/affiliations/credentials are published alongside articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Open reports may include timestamped review histories consisting of referee reports and author rebuttals or a letter from the editor integrating reviewers’ comments; they may be mandated, optional (decided by the author or editor), or not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports are the second core element of OPR transparency. Important to capture what is published (original reports vs. consolidated letters), timing of publication (pre-, concurrent, or post-publication), and access location (alongside article, separate volume, repository). Measure whether reports are consistently available and whether they include full review histories and rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: core elements defining OPR transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Across the variations in OPR implementations, two important factors define the degree of transparency: open identities and open reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence and whether each core element is mandated or optional to place journals along a transparency continuum. Record combinations (e.g., both required, identities optional/reports mandated, identities-only, neither).

rubrics_metrics.name: who decides about open elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An OPR journal needs to decide who makes decisions regarding openness: reviewer, author, and editor/journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating implementations, document which actor has the decision power for open identities and open reports (reviewer chooses to sign, author chooses to publish reports, editor mandates). This affects the process–product configuration and transparency level.

rubrics_metrics.name: when the decision is made (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the decision is made for a specific core element: pre-, post-, or concurrent process (e.g., pre-publication, synchronous, post-publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing influences transparency — concurrent open review (as in F1000Research) is most transparent because reports and identities are available during review; post-publication or after acceptance reduces process transparency. Record timing for each journal's OPR implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: what is contained in open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: What is contained in open reports: original reports, a consolidated letter, or invited commentaries by reviewers who made significant contributions to the paper’s revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the content richness of open reports — whether full referee reports and author rebuttals are published, or only editor summaries/integrated letters. This affects interpretability and reusability of review material.

rubrics_metrics.name: where open reports can be accessed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the open reports can be accessed: alongside the article, in a stand-alone volume, or deposited to third-party services (e.g., Publons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility location affects discoverability and permanence. Document whether reports are displayed with the article, archived separately, or rely on external platforms, and whether access is immediate or delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: process–product approach to OPR
rubrics_metrics.description: A descriptive framework focusing on how open identities and open reports are being fulfilled during the review process (process) and what end products are available for open access (product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the review process transparency (who sees what when) and the published artifacts (reports, rebuttals, histories). Use both axes to classify implementations (e.g., concurrent process + full product vs. closed process + identities-only product).

rubrics_metrics.name: transparency continuum / levels of implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: OPR implementations vary across a continuum from fully transparent (open identities + open reports + open process) to minimal implementations (e.g., published reviewer names only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place journals on a transparency continuum: fully open (e.g., F1000Research concurrent open review), both open identities and reports published post-acceptance (e.g., many BMC journals), mandated reports but optional identities (e.g., Kowsar), optional identities and reports (e.g., PeerJ), or identities-only (e.g., Frontiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: adoption and growth metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics to track OPR adoption: number of OPR journals, year of first OPR use, trend over time, disciplinary distribution, and publisher contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect quantitative indicators (counts, percentages, growth rates) by discipline and publisher. The paper tracked 617 OPR journals as of 2019, first-adopter years, and showed greater prevalence in Medical and Health Sciences. Publishers should add OPR metric data to annual reports (e.g., percentage of articles with open reports/identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: policy classification for identity and report availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify journal policy for reviewer identity (required/optional/anonymous) and policy for report availability (required/optional/not available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabulate frequency of each policy type. The study recorded that 98.5% of OPR journals required or allowed reviewer identification and 86.9% required or allowed open reports; only 30.6% required both. Use these policy categories for systematic comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: additional OPR elements (beyond core)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other OPR elements identified by Ross-Hellauer: open participation, open interaction, open pre-review manuscripts, open final-version commenting, and open platforms/decoupled review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing OPR comprehensively, include whether journals support these additional elements (e.g., crowd-sourced review, public commenting on preprints, decoupled review platforms). The study excluded journals that implemented only these secondary elements from its core dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: data verification and inclusion criteria for OPR identification
rubrics_metrics.description: OPR journal identification requires verifying publisher/journal webpages and issues to confirm open identities or open reports; journals were included only if at least one core element was implemented and evidence found as of a cutoff date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on directory metadata (DOAJ, Transpose) because records may be misclassified or outdated. Manually inspect issues and policy pages; note the year of first OPR use from issue content or explicit publisher statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: discoverability and policy transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should make their OPR information (policies, open reports, open identities) more accessible and should more prominently display their OPR status and adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should record the ease of locating OPR policies and status on publisher/journal websites. Poor visibility/buried policies hinder accurate identification and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: user attitudes and usage indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys of authors, reviewers and editors measure attitudes (comfort with signing, preference for open reports vs identities) and usage metrics (clicks to review reports) to assess impact and acceptance of OPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include survey-derived measures (percent comfortable with open identities/reports, willingness to sign) and usage statistics (report views/clicks) as evaluative dimensions of OPR effectiveness and uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: disciplinary and regional adoption patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: OPR adoption varies by discipline (most prevalent in Medical and Health Sciences and Natural Sciences) and publisher geography (notably high representation of European-based publishers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing implementations, account for disciplinary cultures and regional differences; humanities and technology fields showed lower mandatory open report adoption. Use discipline-level breakdowns to contextualize adoption rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: third-party deposit and reviewer-led publication of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Review reports may be published by reviewers via third-party services (e.g., Publons) where reviewers decide to make their reports public, sometimes in partnership with publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether journals/publishers support or partner with third-party repositories for reviews, and whether the decision to publish reports is contingent on reviewer action rather than author/publisher policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: need for an OPR registry and standard metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Current indexing sources (DOAJ, Transpose) are limited and frequently incorrect; a repository or registry of OPR journals that provides key elements relevant to OPR is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for a standardized registry capturing core OPR elements, adoption year, publisher, policies, and per-article metrics; use such registries for systematic monitoring and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: content-based assessment of open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The next phase of research involves examining open report contents using text mining approaches to determine quantitative and qualitative differences based on OPR models; a scoring instrument is being developed and tested to measure different models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For production or evaluation, implement content analysis / scoring instruments to compare review quality, constructiveness, length, tone, and substantive differences across OPR implementations. Consider automated text-mining metrics plus manual coding.
